chapter_theme: The fourth ten, Kappiyaatru Kappiyanar's songs for Kalangaaykkanni Narmudi Cheral: a festival of Vishnu framing the king who set the shaken peoples right, a conqueror not angry in the enemy's land, an army that is its own fortress, the blood-field as the king's unfailing wealth, an unbent rule beside victory, a king who will not eat sweet things alone, and a dancer guided to the slayer of Nannan, who gives war elephants; the preface adds his birth, the Poozhi conquest and Nannan's beheading.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's rule, body, queen and army

31.reading: The poet sets the king among scenes of a sacred festival, where fasting crowds from the four quarters, to the clang of bells, bathe at the cold ghat and praise the red feet of the lord with the tulasi garland and the discus before going home glad, and tells him that like the full moon driving off the dark he set the shaken peoples right and took the drum, that his chest is like the cloud-soaked mountain and his shoulders like the bar of the sky fortress, that he is like the rich and famous Vandan, that his queen is like the red star among the women of the sky, and that his army, which never strikes a fleeing back, is a shield to friends and a terror to foes.
31.nuance: The first ten lines are a festival of Vishnu with no word yet about the king; the poem then turns to him through the moon simile, so the worshippers' joy at the god's feet becomes the frame for the people's relief under the king. The queen is praised in the same breath as his body and army (lines 23 to 28), as the red star (செம்மீன்) that tradition names Arundhati, the model of chastity. Line 33 (புறக்கொடை எறியார்) states the rule of not striking a fleeing back as a trait of his soldiers.

comparisons.tenor: the king who set the shaken peoples right, as the full moon drives off the dark
the king's broad ornamented chest

comparisons.vehicle: தூங்(கு)எயில் கதவம் காவல் கொண்ட எழூஉநிவந்(து) அன்ன
comparisons.tenor: the king's drum-like strong shoulders
the king, rich and famous through the world
the queen of the old city, chief in chastity
the king's army as it falls on enemies

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's virtues and one wonder in particular

32.reading: The poet says the king's virtues are too many to count, his fame and rectitude that light the quarters, his wealth that gives until it is spent so that his kin rejoice, and the victory that set the shaken peoples right, yet one thing amazes him: having broken the enemy's strength and camped with mountain-like elephants to ruin their land, and having taken their country of sure harvests where the heron feeds in the paddy among canes, the king is not angry even in the land of those foes who reviled him.
32.nuance: The praise turns on restraint, not ferocity: the conquest is told in a few lines so that the closing wonder (இறும்பூதால் பெரிதே) can fall on the absence of anger where it could be used. The counting pebbles failing (இடுகழங்கு தபுந, line 8) is a counting game used as a measure of the king's virtues.

comparisons.tenor: the king's elephants

thinai_evidence.note: the army marches into enemy land, camps and ties its elephants to the guardian tree

33.reading: The poet tells the lord of the bannered chariot that, when his army ties its belled, palm-legged elephants to the enemy's guardian tree, muddies the deep fords and camps all around like an endless flood that ruins the land, it is itself a fortress, with swords for its wall, raised spears for its thorn hedge, the red points of arrows for its moat and drums that roar like thunder, a fort that moves on foot, and kings who would face him in war shrink from him once they think of it.
33.nuance: The poem builds a fortress out of the marching army, part by part, so the king who breaks walls needs none of his own. Tying war elephants to the enemy's guarded tree (கடிமரம்) is the insult that opens the war; the decade's preface tells how the king cut down Nannan's guardian vakai.

comparisons.tenor: the strong legs of the elephants
the king's wide army
the army as a fortress of swords, spears and arrows
the roar of the war drums

thinai_evidence.note: the clash of two kings' armies and the king's power to overcome them

34.reading: The poet says kings shun the great king because, when warriors with anklets and robes trailing to the ground come on red-maned horses, on long-bannered chariots and on the necks of gold-decked elephants with blazing forehead plates, he wears down the stand of unyielding men, breaks the great drummed battle amid rising shouts and overcomes kings, and so the noble young man guards his people.
34.nuance: Line 8 is a gap in the text, so what the warriors of lines 2 to 7 are set against is lost; the chain of three mounts (horse, chariot, elephant) gives the three arms of the enemy force before the gap. The last line (ஓம்பல் மாறே) gives guarding as the reason for the victories, and is the line the next poem begins from.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's battlefield is praised as his wealth

35.reading: The poet says the king's victories are worth telling: on the wide field where great elephants lie with their shining tusks, chariot wheels have run over them and crested birds will not go in with their flocks, where headless bodies dance on the battleground and the square of blood glows red like the evening sky, demons dance, and that conquering war is his unfailing wealth.
35.nuance: The closing line calls the blood-field itself the king's unfailing abundance (வீயா யாணர்), a word used of fertile land; the battlefield is praised as a field that never stops yielding. The dancing headless bodies (மெய்ஆடு, line 6) are the கவந்தம் of later war poetry.

comparisons.tenor: the battlefield red with blood

thinai_evidence.note: the slaughter of the field is told to the victor

36.reading: The poet tells the king, whose wealth never fails, that with a glad heart he overcame fresh battles at the head of mighty warriors, and in the fierce vanguard where swords clashed many elephants fell with their trunks cut like palms in a cleared field, the grey-backed vulture with its mate and spotted neck and the hawk carried off the flesh of fallen horses and men, fearsome demons bearing long rows of the dead ate and danced in joy, and red blood ran, so he makes many wars; long live his wealth.
36.nuance: The cleared palm field (பனைதடி புனம், line 5) turns the felled elephants into farm work, as the kalavazhi thurai, named after the threshing floor, tends to do. The male vulture paired with its mate (பெடைபுணர் சேவல்) keeps a love-poem image in a scene of carrion.

comparisons.tenor: elephants felled with their trunks cut
the spotted neck of the vulture

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's victory and his straight rule

37.reading: The poet blesses the king's wealth and life, as truthful men praise his fame: he gives grief in full to enemies and scatters fine jewels in full to friends, a restrained and calm chief without fault whose fame breathes with the world; he has the victory that set the shaken peoples right, wears the dark palm garland and great anklets, breaks kings' forts and upholds his warriors, and keeps an unbending rule set straight for those who live in his shade; this the fierce king has in great measure for the people of the world.
37.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 balance in one pattern (பகைவர் ஆர / நகைவர் ஆர): grief for foes and gifts for friends are given in the same full measure. The rule is described with the bending metaphor twice over (கோடற வைத்த கோடாக் கொள்கை), so straightness is set beside the victory as a second possession.

comparisons.tenor: the king's protection of those who live under him

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's fame and his living for others

38.reading: The poet says many in the world are rich but the king's fame exceeds them all, Kalangaaykkanni Narmudi Cheral who set right the country where wealth had been thrown into confusion, lord of elephants with ringed tusks and red-maned horses, king of the Cheras, the wealth of suppliants, the day-court of bards, husband of the bright-browed queen, bull among warriors, of scarred and spotless chest, Vaanavaramban, because, with a heart free of the flaw that wishes sweet things to be given so each may enjoy them alone, he has gathered the manliness of sharing food and lives for others.
38.nuance: Sharing food is called manliness (பகுத்(து)ஊண் தொகுத்த ஆண்மை), placed among the war titles as one more of them. Lines 5 and 6 may play on தோட்டி, the goad that drives the elephant against the fort gate and perhaps also the name of the fort it won; the second sense cannot be settled from this text.

comparisons.tenor: the king among warriors
the king as the wealth of suppliants

thinai_evidence.note: the king's fury in the thumbai battle against unsubmissive forts

39.reading: The poet says that because the king lives for others, the band who tell his valour never say they lack anything: in the hot thumbai battle, while the war drum roars like thunder, the guarded front of the angry foes cries out and the forts of the unyielding wither as he goes, fierce as Death; and in the mantle of green gold set with gems, woven not of thread but fine as hair, bright as lightning and sewn with pearls, like the spider's web hung on the dry branches of the velam tree where the flock of grey-backed, spotted-necked doves cries, they delight in the shade of his war.
39.nuance: The syntax of lines 9 to 16 is hard: the gold mesh that is like a spider's web on a thorn tree seems to be the king's war mantle, and the crying doves are the frightened enemy's land, but the connection of the parts is not certain. The shade of war (போர்நிழல்) that the band delights in is the next poem's opening.

comparisons.tenor: the war drum
the king's fierce strength
the mantle of gold mesh
the spotted neck of the doves

thinai_evidence.note: the poem guides a dancer to the king who will give elephants

40.reading: Praying that the king's army, which with its kin delights in the shade of war, may never turn back from a town's front, the poet tells how it camped in ripe fields where karanthai spread, silenced the warriors of the kings' forts, killed and won the hard battle of crowned kings, filled the people and danced the victory, under Narmudi Cheral who cut down at the guarded root the flame-flowered vakai of Nannan of the golden chariot, who rejoices in the toddy he gives while strained liquor holds back suppliants, lord of Neri hill; and he tells the small-bangled dancer that if she goes, adorned like the flowering vengai, with bards in fresh flowers and young men praising the wide field, he will give her many trained war elephants.
40.nuance: The guide poem gives the dancer war elephants, not jewels or food: the spoils of the battle in the first half are what the patron hands out in the second. Line 17 (புன்கால் உன்னம் சாய) names the unnam tree, which droops as an omen of defeat for the king's foes. The felling of Nannan's vakai (line 15) is the deed the decade's preface makes its centre.

comparisons.tenor: the dancer's shining ornaments

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's birth and conquests

patikam:4.reading: The decade's preface says that Kalangaaykkanni Narmudi Cheral, son of Cheralathan of unfailing fortune by the queen of Padhuman, lord of the Vel Aavi line, was born to make the battle front tremble, grew in fame, took the Poozhi country by war, cut off the head of Nannan of Peruvaayil in a pitched battle, felled the whole trunk of his gold-bearing vakai, made the red flood of blood drag elephants, fought many battles, performed the sacrifice of the red field and set the shaken peoples right; and that Kappiyaatru Kappiyanar sang this ten.
patikam:4.nuance: The preface supplies what the songs only touch: his parentage, the Poozhi conquest and the killing of Nannan, which 40 mentions only through the felled vakai. The battlefield sacrifice (செங்களம் வேட்டு) and the shaken peoples set right (துளங்குகுடி திருத்திய) repeat the songs' own formulas (32, 37).

comparisons.tenor: the blood of the battlefield

links.note: Kural 301 says anger is truly restrained only where it could take effect; Patitruppattu 32 marvels that the king, having broken the enemy and taken their land, is not angry even in the country of those who reviled him.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule names the only test of restraint that counts, and the Chera poem shows a king passing it at the one moment conquest gives his anger full power, which is why the poet calls it a wonder rather than a duty.

links.note: Kural 750 says that whatever excellences a fort has, it is nothing without men excellent in action; Patitruppattu 33 makes the marching army itself a fortress, swords for wall, spears for hedge and arrows for moat.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the defenders the real worth of a fort, and the Chera poet takes that to its end by removing the walls altogether, so that the fort exists wherever the army camps.

links.note: Purananuru 62 asks what winning a war can mean when both kings die, and shows demon women dancing in the blood of the dead; Patitruppattu 35 shows demons dancing in the red field and calls that war the king's unfailing wealth.
links.teaches: The same picture of demons dancing on the blood-field is proof of glory when a victor lives to be praised and proof of futility when no one is left to take the field, so the image itself carries no verdict and the surviving king supplies it.

links.note: Purananuru 369, a kalavazhi for another Chera, maps the battle onto rain and tillage, with elephants as clouds and chariots as ploughs; Patitruppattu 36, also kalavazhi, has the elephants fall with trunks cut like palms in a cleared field.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show the kalavazhi of the Chera court treating slaughter as farm work, a single cleared-field simile in one poem and a full season of ploughing and harvest in the other, so the thurai's name from the threshing floor shapes its images.

links.note: Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the sceptre that does not bend; Patitruppattu 37 lists the king's victory (வலம்படு வென்றியும்) and his unbending principle (கோடாக் கொள்கையும்) as two separate things he has.
links.teaches: The Kural makes straight rule the cause of victory, while the Chera poet sets the two side by side as distinct possessions, so the praise poem lacks the causal claim the maxim adds and shows the two were first counted as separate royal goods.

links.note: Kural 322 ranks sharing food (பகுத்துண்டு) first among all that the authors gathered (தொகுத்தவற்றுள்); Patitruppattu 38 praises the king for the manliness that gathered the sharing of food (பகுத்(து)ஊண் தொகுத்த ஆண்மை) and for living for others.
links.teaches: The same pair of words, sharing and gathering, ranks a virtue in the Kural's list of teachings and names a king's acquired valour in the Chera poem, so a virtue the Kural places among the vows against killing appears here as a warrior's manhood.

links.note: Purananuru 182 says the world endures because there are people who will not eat even nectar alone and who strive for others, not for themselves; Patitruppattu 38 says the king has no wish to enjoy sweet things alone and lives for others.
links.teaches: The Purananuru gives an unnamed class of people on whom the world rests, and the Chera praise gives the same refusal to eat alone to one named king, which shows the court poet drawing on a general moral picture to make the patron its single instance.

links.note: Akananuru 199 measures the wealth a man refuses to leave his wife for by the land Narmudi Cheral regained when Nannan fell in the battle at the great ford of the vakai; Patitruppattu 40 praises the same Narmudi Cheral for cutting down Nannan's vakai at the root.
links.teaches: The love poem adds that the country won from Nannan was one the Chera had lost before (இழந்த நாடு), which the praise poem does not say, and it shows the king's greatest gain already serving akam poets as the very largest wealth a lover could turn down.

links.note: Kuruntokai 73 says the Kosar killed Nannan's fragrant mango tree and drove him from his land; the preface of the fourth ten says Narmudi Cheral beheaded Nannan of Peruvaayil and felled his gold-bearing vakai.
links.teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on which tree was Nannan's guardian and who destroyed him, so either the name Nannan covers more than one chief or felling his guarded tree was a victory several conquerors claimed, and neither poem alone shows that the deed was told of more than one enemy.

source_issues: 31-40: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); 33 is marked vanji, 34 and 39 thumbai, 35 and 36 vaakai, the rest paadaan. 39's colophon says வாகை, but the poem's matter is the thumbai battle and the forts that wither.
31 line 25 was supplied from sangamtamil.com (flag: eye-skip in our source joined two lines).
33 line 1 reads இறும்பூதால் பரிதே, but the decade's linked openings repeat 32's last line, இறும்பூதால் பெரிதே; பரிதே is likely a misprint.
33 line 6 நரிதரும் is probably a misprint for நெரிதரும் (crushing); the line is read that way here.
34 line 8 is a lacuna (dots in the source); 34 line 10 முரை(சு) is likely a misprint for முர(சு).
37 line 7 துளங்குடி for துளங்குகுடி (32 line 7, patikam line 12) looks like a dropped syllable; 37 line 9 தாணஇத் is unclear and may be corrupt.
36 line 8 and 39 line 10 share the line பொறித்த போலும் புள்ளி எருத்தின் (flagged), applied to a vulture in 36 and to doves in 39.
Repaired lines (flags): 32 line 17 (TSCII leftover) and 40 line 4 (stray space); both readings are plausible.
patikam:4 line 14 (காப்பியாற்றுக் காப்பியனார் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.
